Horses and People Magazine • Month 2017 • 19 The Moyle Horse of Idaho WORDS BY Kerry Morgan, BA Dip Ed In collaboration with Marilynn Moyle, DVM I started on the quest to ind out about horses possessing ‘horns’; more accurately, frontal skull bosses (small bony bumps covered by skin and hair that occur on the forehead) ater reading the following sentence in a 2007 aricle by Beverly Davis11: “Bucephalus means ‘ox-head’ and it is possible the name might come from the calcium ‘horns’ that are found on the foreheads of horses descended from the Persian.” My research led me to the Moyle horse, a rare breed which was known to regularly exhibit these frontal skull bosses... The Moyle was and is a rare breed of horse developed by ranchers Rex Moyle (1913–1992) and Marjorie Moyle (nee Uhl, 1921–2015), beginning in the 1930’s. Rex Moyle was originally from a Mormon family in Utah, but later moved to Idaho. The horses came from Mormon Pony Express stock, renowned for their speed and endurance, mixed later on with infusions of Cleveland Bay and some Thoroughbred, which contributed to size, bone and high incidence of bay colour; though, in recent imes, buckskins were also favoured on the home ranch. Originally called by their breeder ‘Pony Express’ horses 29, the Moyle horses demonstrated excepional endurance, compeing in the Tevis Cup and other long-distance races with success in the era from the early 1960’s to the end of the 1980’s (See Table 1 in the online version at htp://bit.ly/2kXSets). In appearance, they were between 14 and 16 hands, with good bone, large, hard black feet, long lat musculature, with the foreleg set far forward and ine short coats most frequently bay in colour (though other colours occurred, such as buckskin, brown, black, grey and chestnut, oten with a metallic sheen) . There were few, if any, white markings, and the horses usually had a sparse mane and tail. The horses possessed quite large, plain heads, someimes with frontal skull bosses. Many Moyle horses were gaited, being able to pace or ‘singlefoot’, and possessing a long walking stride. There are a handful of Moyle horses sill in existence, mostly in the hands of the Moyle family. Peculiarities of the Moyle horse The most obvious unusual feature possessed by some Moyle horses are frontal skull bosses. These are small bony bumps covered by skin and hair that occur on the forehead. If you drew diagonal lines from the eye socket to the base of the ear, these bumps most oten occur equidistantly along the two diagonal lines. These bony bumps are evident on the skull of a deceased Moyle horse. The skull bosses may not be signiicant to the horse in terms of funcion or appearance, but they make an impression on the observer, looking very similar to the horn buds seen on calves. Frontal skull bosses have been observed in other horse breeds, the author having collected photographs of a number of Thoroughbreds and Warmbloods, two Saddlebreds, and some horses of unknown breeding that possess them. An aricle published in 1934 by S. Harmstead Chubb14 includes photographs of two heavy work horses which possess frontal bosses, and there is a photograph of a cast of the forehead of a 3-year-old Thoroughbred. As well as the Moyle, the bosses are said to have been seen in the Carthusian Andalusian and the Datong of China 15. Skull bosses usually occur in pairs but, someimes, a horse may have just one - if there is one, it is commonly present in the same posiion along the axes described above. Horses and People Magazine • Month 2017 • 2120 • www.horsesandpeople.com.au A World OF HORSES There are other unusual conformaion features that disinguish the Moyle horse. These, according to Rex Moyle17,15 included an observed higher percentage of red meat/muscle - around 54%, compared to a igure of around 42% to 46% for other breeds of horses. The spleen (the organ used for iltering blood) and the liver were also much larger, as was the heart 19. Forearms were set much further forward on the frame and the shoulder assembly was supported by a ‘sling’ of muscle, enabling a greater range of movement in the front end, a feature that can be seen as ‘Silky’ climbs Cougar Rock in the 1971 Tevis Cup in Image A. [It should be noted that Rex Moyle, as part of the Moyle Mink Ranch, was accustomed to butchering horses and had the opportunity to compare internal structures of the occasional culled Moyle horse with corresponding organs from a variety of other breeds of horses shipped in to the ranch for meat. Rex Moyle, through his understanding of geneics and extensive record-keeping, systemaically developed new colours of mink, such as pastel, violet, aleuian, demi and black.] These peculiariies of musculo-skeletal conformaion and internal organs enabled Moyle horses to have a greater range of lateral movement and lexibility, according to their breeder. Moyle stated the horses had “their ribs curved more at the top and had a deeper valley along the backbone for the other muscles to it into… Their strength was kind of packed and hidden down inside them” 17. They had large plain heads, someimes with an arched proile and Roman nose, and ears set low that could give a slightly lop-eared appearance. Opinions on the temperament of the Moyle horses vary - some members of the family regarded them as a ‘horseman’s horse’; tough, self- reliant, brave, curious and independent, able to form bonds with their own rider, but not always tolerant of strangers - a legacy perhaps of their Mustang heritage. Moyles also appear to have had natural ability as endurance mounts, with a high degree of success in events such as the Tevis Cup; they achieved some remarkable results, given that only a handful of these horses had the opportunity to compete and, in the early days, this was without being given any special training or preparaion 10,17,23. The origins of the Moyle horse Stories of the Mormon Pony Express horses told of their ability to far outlast other ridden horses and carriage horses of the era13. The irst of the Mormon line of horses owned by the Moyle family was ‘Hansen’, whose dam was acquired by Rex Moyle’s grandfather from a Mormon rider. In 1877-78, there was a controversial murder trial concerning the Mountain Meadow Massacre, which had occurred 20 years earlier. The rider sent by O.P. Rockwell to warn Brigham Young of the approach of the United States cavalry marshalls over-ran his horse. The mare “gave out” at the Hansen’s place - it turned out she was in foal - and the messenger agreed under pressure to swap her for a fresh horse to take him the 12 miles to Provo, where he could obtain a replacement mount. The mare later gave birth to a illy who was named ‘Hansen’ and was given to Rex Moyle’s mother, Mailda Charlota Hansen [Moyle], as a dowry git17,20. Hansen had 16 foals, all of them colts who became ranch geldings. This line of horses were the ones the young Rex Moyle grew up with and, when the last of them “ran out” in the 1930’s, he discovered ranch mounts of other breeds could not match the qualiies of these special family horses. “The neighbours also hired cowboys and a working string was usually eight to 10 horses per man. On the Moyle ranch, the cowboys got one horse per man and were usually beter mounted…The Moyle horse could work catle all day without needing a rest.” (Hendricks, 1995) Moyle was inspired to ind and preserve the Mormon Pony Express bloodlines. Himself coming from pioneering Mormon stock, he knew on good authority that Porter Rockwell had released some of the horses in the Cedar Mountains of Utah, and determined to locate and capture some of the Mustangs that it the type to use as breeding stock. The Mormon Pony Express horses Rex Moyle had made his own study of the history of the horses and set down his thoughts in a document in 1990, typed for him by his wife as, by that ime, he sufered from glaucoma. “In 1861… The Pony Express bought horses from a Mormon named Kimball who wrote in his diary that he received $250 per head at a ime when the best horses in the East could be bought for $40 per head. “The Pony Express went in with O.P. Rockwell to raise these good horses for them. Rockwell sent away for seven stallions. I can’t get the records, but I am sure they were from Russia arriving via California. My father knew of one stallion kept at the Warm Springs, Utah staion about 20 miles south of Salt Lake. The other six were turned loose at Rockwell’s ranch on Government Creek near Skull Valley.” Rex Moyle said of his horses, “I have found they are mainly a kind of a one- person animal - friendly to their rider and not so to anyone else. I have found in a real old book about horses in the New York Library an account of a brown horse raised deep in Eastern Asia (Russia?) by a noble family for 450 or more years for war purposes. These horses were selected for the ones to go through the batle lines, while the rider shot arrows or gun… This horse would only accept the rider or corral master - kicking, striking or biing anyone unknown to him… I believe these may be some of our horses’ ancestors…” (Rex Moyle, unpublished 1990 document, copy provided by the Moyle family). People who know about the history of horses may connect the dots here... The foundaion horse Rex Moyle described was very likely the Turkoman (also Turk, Turkmene, Teke, and known by other names at various periods in history), legendary as the quintessenial warhorse of Central Asia and Eastern Europe, and prized through aniquity. In the pedigree of the English Thoroughbred, there are numerous animals that bear the name ‘Turk’ - the Byerley Turk being just one of them [The well-researched historical novel ‘The Byerley Turk’ by Jeremy James, 2005, provides an insight into the history of this stallion and the breed]. These horses were inaccurately described as “Arabs”, but were brought back to England as part of the ‘spoils of war’ ater encounters with the Turkish military in the Crimea and elsewhere from the 16th Century. It should be menioned the Turkoman of the 1600’s–1800’s was not as lean or atenuated as some of the modern types of Akhal-Teke, having more bone and substance. Horses and People Magazine • Month 2017 • 2322 • www.horsesandpeople.com.au In 1935, 15 Turkoman horses of the Akhal-Teke line made a forced march from Ashkabad to Moscow, crossing approximately 299 miles of the Kara Kum desert without water 4. It is interesing to note a website describing the Turkoman menions the Mormon Horse and the Moyle horse as some “possible Turks in the Americas” 24. In 1990, Professor E. Gus Cothran, PhD, analysed samples from Moyle horses which showed “strong relaionship to the Spanish horse” 15, in addiion to some “unique markers” 19. This may not be surprising given the consistent addiion of Mustang blood to the old Mormon lines over the decades. The Moyle is a unique breed in its own right - being a mixture of inluences honed over decades in harsh, tesing range condiions, along with the linebreeding program created by Rex Moyle. Blood samples from 15 Moyle horses were submited in March 2016 and advances in modern geneic analysis techniques may be able to more accurately pinpoint the diferent elements of the origin of the breed. Bonnie Hendricks (1995) notes: “A contact of mine in Turkey wrote to say that, 20 years ago [i.e. 1970’s], he met a man with three horses he had obtained in Persia that had the same small knobs on their foreheads and he called them “Dragon Horses”. He was told they were extremely rare.” Louise Firouz (1933-2008), the notable American horsewoman who married into the Iranian Royal Family and moved to Iran, made eforts to ind and preserve the Turkoman horse, formerly regarded as lost. She is also known as the person who singlehandedly resurrected the Caspian breed 20. (See also the Caspian feature in Horses and People Magazine: htps:// www.horsesandpeople.com.au/aricle/ the-caspian). [It should be noted that, in the Turkoman, Akhal-Teke or Caspian horse, examples of frontal skull bosses have not, thus far, been photographed or observed - apart from the reference by Hendricks above.] Rex Moyle, quoted in Pony Express magazine, April 1965 28, stated in regard to the horses’ ancestry, that “Rockwell obtained ancestors of this breed at Monterey from a boat arriving on January 18, 1848.” Eforts to idenify the vessel and the source of its equine cargo have, thus far, been unsuccessful. What we have are lines of enquiry that point in several direcions - some of the foundaion stock for the Mormon Pony Express horses were imported “from overseas”, and there is documentary support for this having happened. Pony Express horses were notable for their outstanding speed and endurance, veriied by records, to the point of having atained legendary status for the brief period during which the service operated 13; the Hansen line of horses were direct descendants of a working Mormon mare of Pony Express lines; Rex Moyle’s later bloodlines were sourced from Cedar Mountain Mustang herds, based on his knowledge of Rockwell’s acions and on his own judgement of the ‘type’ he was ater; Moyle believed the horses to be descended from stock imported from “Eastern Asia”; Moyle horses of the 1960’s-1980’s have proven performance in endurance compeiion 1,2,3,10,17,21 (See also Table 1 at: htp://bit.ly/2kXSets); autopsy data veriied by qualiied veterinarians support the claims of “unusual conformaional qualiies” both internal and external; analysis of blood samples taken in 1990 showed Spanish Mustang markers, whilst more discriminaing tests on bloods taken in 2016 are currently pending. Those skull bosses... How and why do equine skull bosses occur, how frequently do they appear? There have been references in aniquity to ‘horned horses’, the most notable being Alexander’s Bucephalus (‘ox- 11. Scholars have generally dismissed these as being associated with myths, cults, religion and so on. Such references may or may not have been based on horses with skull bosses. A paper published in 1934 , ‘Frontal Protuberances in Horses – An Explanaion of the So-Called ‘Horned’ Horse’ by S. Harmstead Chubb14 suggests that, in some horses with a paricular kind of skull conformaion, during foetal development there is pressure at usually two (someimes one) areas of the underside of the forehead secion of the skull, where the carilaginous edges of the wings of the orbitosphenoid may, for a ime, penetrate the frontal area of the skull, with one or two calciied ‘bumps’ developing at the site of this transient phase. Equine skeletal specialist Dr Deb Bennet has suggested frontal skull bosses are bony overgrowths at junctures of the skull plates, and are associated with a straight or convex proile. Dr Bennet also believes the Greek term ‘ox-head’ referred to a paricular head type in ancient horses with a broad forehead and large eyes. Examinaion of a Moyle skull by Marilynn Moyle, DVM did not, however, show any irregulariies on the underside of the bone corresponding to the locaion of the bumps on the frontal aspect. Marilynn Moyle has observed the bosses appear more deined on a young horse and, in some cases, seem to become less pronounced as the horse matures - photographs of ‘Moyle Obknoxious’ over several years, and before and ater gelding, show the skull bumps as quite disinct when the horse was four years old (See image A), to being barely visible in photographs of him as an 8-year-old gelding, though bosses were sill present. Horses and People Magazine • Month 2017 • 2524 • www.horsesandpeople.com.au The mares and intact stallions appear to retain the frontal bosses. Ater castraion and loss of testosterone, the bosses appear to be resorbed (osteoporosis). ‘Moyle Moxie’, whilst not possessing skull bosses, has two hair whorls on her forehead over the sites where bosses would appear. In what may be a world irst, in August 2016, ‘Moyle Obknoxious’ went to Washington State University where he underwent a scan under anaesthesia to obtain CT images of the skull of a live horse possessing frontal bosses (See image D). At the same ime, two Moyle Horse skulls were imaged to analyse the characterisics of the curious frontal bosses (See image B). Marilynn Moyle comments, on examinaion of examples of live horses, of conserved skulls in her possession, and of the CT scans, “The bosses are not near the suture lines on the outside of the skull and are not suture line periosiis. The mares with bosses (‘Goldie’ 30 years, ‘Rosie’ 10 years and an unnamed mature mare) sill have prominent bosses. The bosses on the stallions regress ater castraion.” Dr Moyle also notes, observed on CT scan and examinaion, “The bosses are corical bone with cancellous bone of uniform density - marrow cavity without a separate ossiicaion centre - like the thickened areas of the scapula.” Anecdotal evidence obtained by the author from horse professionals, such as farriers and horse denists, suggests frontal bosses are observed in Thoroughbred horses rarely - perhaps at a rate of around two per 1,000. Research by the author has, thus far, conirmed the bosses can occur in other breeds, some of which have had infusions of Thoroughbred blood over ime in their lines. The presence of skull bosses in Spanish, Chinese or Central Asian horses, could be presumed to be from more ancient origins. What the Moyle horse demonstrates is the incidence of skull bosses in that breed is much higher than their apparently ‘random’ occurrence in some other breeds. By selecing a paricular type from a speciic area and linebreeding for certain physical qualiies, it may be conjectured that Rex Moyle also unintenionally selected for a higher incidence of occurrence of skull bosses. The gene pool would have been limited and it is likely the skull bosses were an incidental artefact - historical documents do not state whether the foundaion stock possessed skull bosses, but they do appear to have possessed the genes to predispose their descendants to having them. Skull bosses seem to have been present in around a quarter to a third of Moyle horses when the herd numbered perhaps 15019. A photo taken circa 1953 shows the stallion Porter with disinct skull bosses23. Moyle Horses in endurance competition Beginning in the 1960’s, and for the next 20 years, members of the Moyle family competed in endurance rides, including the famed Tevis Cup 1,2,10,17,21,26,27,28,29. The 2015 60th anniversary commemoraive issue of Tevis Forum magazine looked back on 1960’s, noing the Moyle breed: “Known for their endurance, the Moyle horses had stamina and interesing bony protuberances, horns, on their faces… [In 1965], four Moyle horses were in the top 20.” [In fact, according to Tevis records, there were ive in the top 20.] Both Mathew Mackay-Smith DVM, author of a number of published aricles on the Moyle horse, and son of the well-known equestrian writer Alexander Mackay-Smith, and Mathew’s wife, Wingate ‘Winkie’ Mackay-Smith, rode Moyle horses to top-ten placings in the Tevis in the 1960’s 1,27. Mathew was an outstanding endurance rider who went on to great achievements in the sport. He was Medical Editor for Equus magazine and one of the ive founding DVMs of the American Associaion of Equine Praciioners (AAEP) 1954. Mathew also wrote for several other prominent horse magazines, and it is largely through his aricles that the Moyle horse became known. Moyle Hawk, originally named Holly’s Hawk, was born 1968 and ridden throughout his endurance career by Marjorie Moyle. He completed over 5,000 compeiive endurance miles in ive years. Hawk has earned from the Endurance Horse Registry its Legion of Merit Award for compleion of 5,000 oicial miles and has also been awarded a permanent place in its presigious Hall of Fame1,2,5. The archives of the MRER Mountain Region Endurance Rider’s website made menion of the Moyle Horse. Prior to the formaion of MRER and during our early years, Rex and Margie Moyle of Idaho bred and rode some truly extra ordinary endurance horses which became known as the “Moyle” horses. The story of this family and their Moyle Horses is one of the great Western adventures, with links to the LDS Church and long distance trips between St. Joseph Missouri and Salt Lake. Some of these horses had horns, but what this really meant was the horses had small frontal bosses (extra bone) above their eyes that stood out [less than three-quarter] inches, and covered with hair. These horses are included in this history because they played such a major role in linking the older events of MRER to our current events. Some of the Moyle blood lines are sill present in current endurance horses. A B D C Mathew Mackay Smith, DVM, knew the family well and rode a Moyle horse in the Tevis to 5th place in 1964 and wrote an aricle about them in the 1964 ‘The Chronicle of the Horse’, documening these marvelous and special horses of the West. At the irst Virginia Dale ride hosted by Dave Nicholson, DVM, Mathew Mackay Smith, DVM, was one of the irst, if not the irst, to have a heart monitor. Its electrodes were the size of your hand... Karen Kroon rode ‘Prety Boy Moyle’ in the 1970’s. Jim Larsh was loved by everyone and a friend of Wendell Robie. Jim went to Australia in 1969 and did the Tom Quilty on ‘Ibn Zata’ in 17 hours and 33 minutes. As he got older, he needed oxygen, so Karen Kroon took his Moyle horse ‘True Grit’ and trained it to carry the oxygen botles, so Jim could start the Tevis one more ime. Unfortunately, he did not inish the last ride.21 In more recent imes, riders including elite endurance compeitor John Crandell III with ‘Moyle Artesian’ and ‘Moyle Apple Cider’, and Tano Gavete riding ‘Moyle Obknoxious’, have competed successfully in endurance1,26,27. Gavete’s most recent win on ‘Knox’ was the Jubilee Ranch 50 Mile in 2014, in 6 hours and 9 minutes. Crandell’s ‘Rammit’ is by ‘Moyle Apple Cider’, out of an Arabian mare, and this buckskin gelding was also ridden in compeiion by Crandell’s mentor, Mathew Mackay-Smith. The future of the Moyle Horse The current status of the breed is that it is extremely rare, with the main herd having been dispersed and bloodlines very unfortunately lost in recent imes. It was the end of an era with the passing of Rex Moyle in 1992, and later Marjorie Moyle in 2015. Sadly, the horses of the old bloodlines were seen as surplus to needs on the ranch and were disposed of just prior to Marjorie Moyle’s death in September 2015. The horses of endurance fame in the period from the 1960’s to 1980’s appear taller and rangier than the more compact modern examples, perhaps due to the more recent addiion of some Quarter Horse outcrosses. Some sill possess the essenial appearance and qualiies of the old Mormon breed, not to menion the skull bosses. There may sill exist descendants of the Rockwell horses among the Mustang herds of Cedar Mountain8. Whilst under general anesthesia at WSU in 2016, cell culture from ‘Moyle Obknoxious’ was harvested for cryopreservaion, and processed at Texas A&M University for cloning and research. Marilynn Moyle has four Moyle Horse geldings and two Moyle mares, one of which is in foal to the last known living Moyle stallion. Enthusiasts of this rare and interesing breed would like to ensure that it does not disappear into history like the vanishing dust from those legendary riders of the Pony Express. For a full list of references and to view a table of Tevis Cup results for years in which Moyle Horses competed please read the online version of this aricle at: htp://bit.ly/2kXSets. Interested in the Moyle Horse or have something to add to the history? Email: moylehorses@outlook.com.
